newsitem.title: USA: Oil, grain prices lead commodities higher.
newsitem.headline: Oil, grain prices lead commodities higher.

text.p: Oil prices rose Wednesday on jitters about Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health and a cold snap in the Northeast.
Grain prices also rallied on weather concerns.
Precious metals closed mixed. Overall, the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures closed up 1.67 points on the day at 243.98.

On Wednesday, Yeltsin's doctors ordered him to stay in the hospital all week due to a bout with pneumonia. The news had Communist rivals of Yeltsin in Russia's parliament calling for a vote for Yelstsin's ouster on the grounds of ill health.
That raised questions about Russia's oil output, the world's third largest, if a power struggle caused turmoil.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, February crude oil closed 84 cents a barrel higher at $25.95 a barrel.
Buoyed by those gains, February heating oil closed up 2.00 cents a gallon at 71.42 cents, and February unleaded gasoline ended 1.81 cents higher at 68.85 cents a gallon.

Heating oil also was boosted by predictions that arctic air would chill the Midwest and Northeast later this week and by Tuesday's weekly American Petroleum Institute statistics showing declines in heating oil stocks in the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market.
Although Wednesday's rally snapped two consecutive days of declines, dealers said prices could drop after the American Petroleum Institute data indicated mostly rising oil stocks.

The institute said gasoline stocks rose 415,000 barrels, compared with expectations of an increase of more than 2 million barrels for the week ended Jan. 10. Crude stocks also grew, rising a larger-than-expected 4.7 million barrels.

A fresh snowstorm in the Midwest sparked buying in grains, partly on concerns about ice-snarled rail and barge transport slowing deliveries. March wheat ended 2-1/4 cents higher at $3.90-1/4 and March corn rose 3 cents to $2.73-3/4.
"The transportation slowdown is potentially a problem; it's going to tighten up the stocks," said Skip Searcy, wheat trading specialist for FIMAT Futures.

January soybeans closed up 10-3/4 cents a bushel at $7.44-1/2 on worries that hot, dry weather in Brazil may damage the young soybean crop and on concerns about tight supplies this year in the United States.
Precious metals futures closed mixed in New York, but not before new contract lows were seen across most of the complex.
"... Things still look problematic for gold," said Mitsui USA bullion dealer Greg Drury.
"We're seeing some physical demand in Southeast Asia but with U.S. inflation low and returns on paper assets good, there is no investor interest," he said.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange's COMEX division February gold ended down $1.50 an ounce at $353.20 after reaching a fresh life-of-contract low of $352.60. March silver ended up 1.0 cent an ounce at $4.685 an ounce but not before posting a new contract low of $4.610.
